{{smaller block|Those persons whose souls are dispersed and ''ungathered'' by reason of a wanton humour to intemperate jesting are apt to be trifling in their religion.
{{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Works (ed. 1835), I. 741.}}}}

¶
'''ungear''' (un-gēr′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''gear.''] To strip of gear; also, to throw out of gear.

'''ungeneraled, ungeneralled''' (un-jen′e̤-rald), ''a.'' Made not general; local; particular. ''Fuller.'' [Rare.]

'''ungenerated''' (un-jen′e̤-rā-ted), ''a.'' Not generated; not brought into being. ''Raleigh.''

'''ungenerous''' (un-jen′e̤-rus), ''a.'' Not generous; not showing liberality or nobility of mind or sentiments; illiberal; ignoble; dishonorable.

{{smaller block|<poem>The victor never will impose on Cato
''Ungen’rous'' terms.</poem>
{{right|''Addison'', Cato.}}}}

'''ungenerously''' (un-jen′e̤-rus-li), ''adv.'' In an ungenerous manner; illiberally; ignobly.

'''ungenial''' (un-jē′nial), ''a.'' Not genial. {{smaller|(''a'') Not favorable to natural growth: as, ''ungenial'' air; ''ungenial'' soils. (''b'') Not kindly; unpleasant; disagreeable; harsh; unsympathetic: as, an ''ungenial'' disposition. (''c'') Not congenial; not suited or adapted. [Rare.]}}

{{smaller block|Critical explanations of difficult passages of Scripture . . . do well for publication, but are ''ungenial'' to the habits and taste of a general audience.
{{right|''Sydney Smith'', in Lady Holland, iii.}}}}

'''ungenitured†''' (un-jen′i-t̮ṳ̄rd), ''a.'' Wanting genitals; wanting the power of propagation; impotent. ''Shak.'', M. for M., iii. 2. 184.

¶
'''ungenteel''' (un-jen-tēl′), ''a.'' Not genteel; impolite; rude: of persons or manners.

'''ungenteelly''' (un-jen-tēl′li), ''adv.'' In an ungenteel manner; impolitely; uncivilly. ''Edinburgh Rev.''

'''ungentle''' (un-jen′tl), ''a.'' [< ME. ''ungentel''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''gentle''.] '''1.''' Not gentle; harsh; rough; rude; ill-bred; impolite.
{{smaller block|When nature biddeth thee to be good and gentle to other, she commandeth thee not to be cruel and ''ungentle'' to thyself. {{right|''Sir T. More'', Utopia (tr. by Robinson), ii. 7.}}
<poem>
Cæsar cannot live
To be ''ungentle.''
</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', A. and C., v. 1. 60.}}}}
'''2.''' Not noble; plebeian.
{{smaller block|Sum man hath grete rychesses, but he is ashamyd of his ''ungentel'' lynage. {{right|''Chaucer'', Boëthius, ii. prose 4.}}}}

'''ungentleman†''' (un-jen′tl-ma̤n), ''v. t.'' Same as ''ungentlemanize''.
{{smaller block|Some tell me home-breeding will ''ungentleman'' him.
{{right|''Gentleman Instructed'', p. 545. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''ungentlemanize''' (un-jen′tl-ma̤n-īz), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''gentleman'' + ''-ize''.] To deprive of the character of a gentleman; make boorish. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Unmanning and ''un-gentlemanizing'' themselves to any extent. {{right|''C. A. Bristed'', English University, p. 416.}}}}

'''ungentlemanlike''' (un-jen′tl-ma̤n-līk), ''a.'' Not like a gentleman; not becoming a gentleman; ungentlemanly. ''Sydney Smith'', To John Allen.

'''ungentlemanliness''' (un-jen′tl-ma̤n-li-nes), ''n.'' The character of being ungentlemanly. ''Quarterly Rev.''

'''ungentlemanly''' (un-jen′tl-ma̤n-li), ''a.'' Not befitting a gentleman; rude; uncivil; ill-bred.

{{smaller block|seasonably ripened doth commonly ''ungive'' afterwards.
{{right|''Fuller'', Ch. Hist., II. ii. 40. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''ungiving''' (un-giv′ing), ''a.'' Not bringing gifts. ''Dryden.'' [Rare.]

'''ungka''', ''n.'' See ''unga.''

'''ungka-puti''' (ung′kä-put-i), ''n.'' [Native name.] The active gibbon of Sumatra, ''Hylobates agilis.'' Also called ''ungha, ungka-pati, ungka-etam.''

'''unglad†''' (un-glad′), ''a.'' [ME. ''unglad'', < AS. ''unglæd'' (= Icel. ''ūgladhr''), not glad; as ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''glad.''] Sorry; sad. ''Alliterative Poems'' (ed. Morris), iii. 63.

'''ungladden''' (un-glad′n), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''gladden.''] To deprive of gladness; leave uncheered; make sad. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|It wears, to my eye, a stern and sombre aspect, too much ''ungladdened'' by genial sunshine.
{{right|''Hawthorne'', Scarlet Letter, p. 49.}}}}

'''unglaze''' (un-glāz′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''glaze.''] To take the glass from, as a window or window-sash.

'''unglazed''' (un-glāzd′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Unprovided with glass, or with glass windows.—'''2.''' Not coated or covered with vitreous matter: as, ''unglazed'' earthenware. See ''unglazed pottery'', under ''pottery.''

'''ungloomed''' (un-glömd′), ''a.'' Not darkened, overshadowed, or overclouded. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|With look ''ungloomed'' by guile. {{right|''M. Green'', The Spleen.}}}}

'''unglorified''' (un-glō′ri-fīd), ''a.'' Not glorified; not honored with praise or adoration. ''Dryden.''

'''unglorify''' (un-glō′ri-fī), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''glorify.''] To deprive of glory. ''Watts'', Remnants of Time, § 31. [Rare.]

{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), iv. 145.}}}}

{{smaller block|''Unglue'' thyself from the world and the vanities of it.

'''unglutted''' (un-glut′ed), ''a.'' Not glutted; not satiated or saturated; not cloyed.

'''ungoard†''', ''a.'' See ''ungored''<sup>1</sup>.

'''ungod'''<sup>1</sup> (un-god′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''ungodded'' ppr. ''ungodding.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''god''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' '''ungod'''<sup>2</sup>†, ''a.'' A Middle English form of ''ungood.''

'''ungodlily''' (un-god′li-li), ''adv.'' In an ungodly manner; impiously; wickedly.

'''ungodly''' (un-god′li), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not godly; careless of God; godless; wicked; impious; sinful: as, ''ungodly'' men or ''ungodly'' deeds. 1 Pet. iv. 18.

'''ungentlemanly''' (un-jen′tl-ma̤n-li), ''a.'' Not befitting a gentleman; rude; uncivil; ill-bred. {{smaller block|Swearing in the Playhouse is an ''ungentlemanly'' as well as an unchristian Practice.
{{right|''Jeremy Collier'', Short View, p. 59.}}}}
='''Syn.''' See ''uncivil.''

'''ungentlemanly''' (un-jen′tl-man-li), ''adv.'' In an ungentlemanly manner; not as a gentleman.
{{smaller block|To defraud and cousen them ''ungentlemanly'' of their parents love, which is the greatest and fairest portion of their inheritance.
{{right|''Holland'', tr. of Plutarch, p. 148.}}}}

'''ungentleness''' (un-jen′tl-nes), ''n.'' '''1.''' Want of gentleness; harshness; severity; rudeness.—'''2.''' Want of politeness; incivility. ''Shak.'', As you Like it, v. 2. 83.

'''ungently''' (un-jent′li), ''adv.'' In an ungentle manner; harshly; with severity; rudely. ''Shak.'', Tempest, i. 2. 444.

'''ungenuine''' (un-jen′ū-in), ''a.'' Not genuine.
{{smaller block|His best Plays are almost always Modest and clear Complexion’d. His Amphitrio, excepting the ''ungenuine'' Addition, is such.
{{right|''Jeremy Collier'', Short View, p. 18.}}}}

'''ungenuineness''' (un-jen′ū-in-nes), ''n.'' The character of being ungenuine; spuriousness.

'''unget''' (un-get′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''get''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''unbeget.''] To treat as if unbegotten. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>I’ll disown you; I’ll disinherit you;
I’ll ''unget'' you.</poem>
{{right|''Sheridan'', The Rivals.}}}}

'''ungifted''' (un-gif′ted), ''a.'' Not gifted. {{smaller|(''a'') Not endowed with peculiar faculties.}}
{{smaller block|A hot-headed, ''ungifted'', unedifying preacher.
{{right|''Arbuthnot'', Hist. of John Bull, xxiii.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') Not having received a gift; without a present. face becomes gilt. {{right|''Workshop Receipts'', 1st ser., p. 196.}}}}

'''ungilded, ungilt''' (un-gil′ded, un-gilt′), ''a.'' Not gilt; not overlaid with gilding.
{{smaller block|Our mean ''ungilded'' stage. {{right|''Dryden.''}}}}

'''ungilding''' (un-gil′ding), ''n.'' The act or process of depriving of gilding; hence, figuratively, a stripping off of decorations.
{{smaller block|By all this wee may conjecture how little wee neede feare that the ''unguilding'' of our Prelates will prove the woodening of our Priests. {{right|''Milton'', Animadversions.}}}}
{{smaller block|Articles of iron, steel, and silver, which cannot be submitted to the ''ungilding''-bath. {{right|''Workshop Receipts'', 1st ser., p. 205.}}}}

'''ungill''' (un-gil′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''gill''<sup>1</sup>.] To release the gills of (a fish) from the net; take or remove from a gill-net, as fish.

'''ungilt†''' (un-gilt′), ''v. t.'' An obsolete variant of ''ungild.''
{{smaller block|Bycause that there was none yll that did ''vngilte'' it. {{right|''Golden Boke'', Prol.}}}}

'''ungiltif†''', ''a.'' [ME.: see ''unguilty.''] Without guilt; innocent.
{{smaller block|<poem>Is this an honour unto thy deyte,
That folk ''ungiltif'' suffren here injure?</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, iii. 1018.}}}}

'''ungird''' (un-gėrd′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''gird.''] To loosen by taking off the girdle, as a robe; also, to take the girdle or belt from.
{{smaller block|The sportive exercises for the which the genius of Milton ''ungirds'' itself. {{right|''Macaulay.''}}}}

'''ungive†''' (un-giv′), ''v.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''give.''] To give way; relax; slacken.
{{smaller block|That religion which is rather suddenly parched up than seasonably ripened doth commonly ''ungive'' afterwards.
{{right|''Fuller'', Ch. Hist., II. ii. 40. (''Davies.'')}}}}

{{smaller block|With look ''ungloomed'' by guile. {{right|''M. Green'', The Spleen.}}}}

'''unglorify''' (un-glō′ri-fī), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''glorify.''] To deprive of glory. ''Watts'', Remnants of Time, § 31. [Rare.]

'''unglosed†''', ''a.'' See ''unglozed.''

It is a small tree, or sometimes a low shrub, with leaves of from 3 to 7 serrate leaflets, the terminal leaflet being long-stalked. To deprive of a god, or cause to recognize no god; make atheistical or godless. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|The wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ''ungodliness.''

'''ungodly''' (un-god′li), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not godly; careless of God; godless; wicked; impious; sinful: as, ''ungodly'' men or ''ungodly'' deeds. 1 Pet. iv. 18.
{{smaller block|<poem>Glory to him whose just avenging ire

{{right|''Milton'', P. L., vii. 185.}}}}
'''2.''' Polluted by wickedness.
{{smaller block|The hours of this ''ungodly'' day.
{{right|''Shak.'', K. John, iii. 1. 109.}} <poem>Such an ''ungodly'' sickness I have got
That he that undertakes my cure must first
O’erthrow divinity, all moral laws.</poem>{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', King and No King, iii. 1.}}}}
'''3.''' Outrageous; extremely annoying. [Slang.]
{{smaller block|The poisonous nature of the wind, and its ''ungodly'' and unintermittent uproar, would not suffer me to sleep.
{{right|''R. L. Stevenson'', Olalla.}}}}
'''4.''' Squeamish; nice. ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.]
{{smaller|='''Syn. 1.''' ''Godless, Unrighteous'', etc. See ''irreligious''.}}

'''ungoodly†''' (un-gůd′li), ''a.'' [< ME. ''ungoodly''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''goodly'', ''a.''] Not goodly; not good; bad.

'''ungoodly†''' (un-gůd′li), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''ungoodly'', ''ongoodly''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''goodly'', ''adv.''] Not well; ill.
{{smaller block|He was ''ongoodly'' servyd ther in.
{{right|''Paston Letters'', III. 125.}}}}

{{smaller block|<poem>Helms of gold
''Vngoard'' with bloud.</poem>{{right|''Sylvester'', The Vacation, p. 288. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''ungored<sup>2</sup>''' (un-gōrd′), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''gore''<sup>2</sup> + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.] Not gored; not wounded as with a horn or spear.
{{smaller block|<poem>I have a voice and precedent of peace,
To keep my name ''ungored''.</poem>{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, v. 2. 261.}}}}

'''ungorged''' (un-gôrjd′), ''a.'' Not gorged; not filled; not sated. {{smaller block|''Ungorged'' with flesh and blood.
{{right|''Dryden'', Theodore and Honoria.}}}}

'''ungorgeous''' (un-gôr′jus), ''a.'' Not gorgeous; not showy or splendid. ''Carlyle'', French Rev., II. iv. 8. (''Davies.'') [Rare.]

'''ungotten, ungot''' (un-got′n, -got′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not gained. ''Daniel'', Civil Wars, vii.—'''2†.''' Not begotten.
{{smaller block|''Ungotten'' and unborn. {{right|''Shak.'', Hen. V., i. 2. 287.}}}}

'''ungovernable''' (un-guv′ėr-na̤-bl), ''a.'' '''1.''' Incapable of being governed, ruled, or restrained; not to be regulated by laws or rules; refractory; unruly.
{{smaller block|So ''ungovernable'' a poet cannot be translated literally.
{{right|''Dryden.''}}
I trust . . . that our enemies, who predict that the indulgence will make us more insolent and ''ungovernable'', may find themselves false prophets.
{{right|''Franklin'', Autobiography, p. 380.}}}}
'''2.''' Licentious; wild; unbridled: as, ''ungovernable'' passions. ='''Syn.''' {{smaller|Unmanageable, intractable, uncontrollable. See ''govern''.}}

'''ungovernableness''' (un-guv′ėr-na̤-bl-nes), ''n.'' The state of being ungovernable.

'''ungovernably''' (un-guv′ėr-na̤-bli), ''adv.'' In an ungovernable manner; so as not to be governed or restrained. ''Goldsmith.''<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
